title: Sort an Array (Merge Sort)
description: Implement merge sort as a reliable O(n log n) divide-and-conquer sort with a stable, predictable worst case.

data.text: Given an array of integers `nums`, sort it in ascending order and return it. You must solve it without using the built-in sort, ideally in `O(n log n)` time with `O(n)` auxiliary space (or `O(log n)` for the recursion stack with in-place merging).

Divide the array in half, recursively sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves. The merge step walks both halves with two pointers, always taking the smaller current element — this is what makes it stable. Recursion depth is `O(log n)` and each level does `O(n)` merge work, giving `O(n log n)` time in every case — worst, average, and best.

data.title: Top-down merge sort O(n log n)

data.caption: Merge sort halves the array down to single elements, then merges sorted pairs back up. Each merge level does O(n) work across O(log n) levels.

data.title: Why not just use Array.Sort?
data.text: Built-in sorts are typically introsort (quicksort + heapsort fallback), which is O(n log n) average but not stable. Merge sort is the go-to when you need guaranteed O(n log n) *and* stability (preserving relative order of equal elements) — the same reason it's the backbone of external sorting and .NET's stable OrderBy.
